sections.summary: Static analysis methods for the nominal resistance of single piles and groups in axial compression, uplift and lateral loading, and the resulting deformations; they set pile type, number and length, and drivability is checked with the wave equation (Chapter 12) at design. Rr = phi_stat Rs + phi_stat Rp (Eq. 7-3), Rs = fs As (Eq. 7-4), Rp = qp Ap (Eq. 7-5). Static phi (Table 7-1): compression 0.35 (alpha), 0.45 (Nordlund), 0.50 (Schmertmann); tension 0.20-0.40. sections.body: 7.1 Introduction (pp. 211-212). Static analysis methods are analytical methods that use geomaterial strength and compressibility properties to determine nominal geotechnical resistance and deformation. The chapter focuses on methods for the nominal geotechnical resistance of single piles and pile groups in axial compression, uplift and lateral loading, and the resulting vertical and lateral deformations. Important considerations: (1) static analysis methods are an integral part of the design process, needed to determine the most cost effective pile type and to estimate the number of piles and the required pile lengths; the designer must know the design loads and project performance criteria. (2) Many methods are available; those presented are relatively simple methods that have provided reasonable agreement with full scale field results, and many are in AASHTO (2014); more sophisticated methods may be used and in some cases give better results; whatever the method, experience from its past field performance should be applied continually. (3) Designers should fully understand the basis, limitations and applicability of a chosen method, particularly computer solutions whose assumptions may not be apparent, and a method should have proven agreement with full scale field results. (4) Evaluation and confirmation of pile drivability is an integral part of limit state design: designs with fewer, larger pile sections of greater nominal resistance are more frequently used, and the ability of these piles to reach the penetration depths needed for all resistance and deformation requirements is a critical design check; a drivability analysis combines this chapter's geotechnical aspects with the wave equation procedures of Chapter 12 and should be performed by the engineer during design. Construction procedures can significantly influence pile behavior: the methods lead to successful designs only with appropriate construction techniques and construction monitoring, which should be integral to design and construction, and static load tests, wave equation analysis or dynamic monitoring for construction control should, whenever possible, confirm a static design. The chapter covers background, static analysis for compression, uplift and lateral loads, pile group settlement, special design events, limited guidance for liquefaction susceptible soils (detailed seismic design is beyond the manual's scope and is in GEC-3, Kavazanjian et al. 2011), and construction issues pertinent to static analysis, using AASHTO (2014) notation and load and resistance factors. Subsections: 7.1.1 Static Analysis Methods in Limit State Design; 7.1.2 Events During and After Pile Driving; 7.1.3 Load Transfer; 7.1.4 Effective Stress; 7.1.5 Resistance Factors; 7.1.6 Interdiscipline Communication and Coordination.

subsections.title: Static Analysis Methods in Limit State Design
subsections.body: There are four general types of static analysis in this chapter (pp. 212-213). They determine: (1) the nominal resistance in axial compression of a pile or pile group - the long-term resistance, the resistance of layers subject to scour, liquefaction or downdrag or otherwise unsuitable for long-term support, the minimum pile penetration, pile lengths for bid quantities, the soil resistance at the time of driving (SRD) and the required nominal driving resistance Rndr; (2) the nominal resistance in axial tension, which in some cases also sets the minimum penetration; (3) the nominal lateral resistance and lateral deformation, by soil-structure interaction methods that also guide pile section selection; and (4) the settlement of a pile group under the structure's service loads. The factored resistance of a pile or pile group is the smaller of the factored geotechnical resistance of the surrounding soil or rock and the factored structural resistance of the pile(s). Vertical (settlement) and lateral deformation of pile groups are computed with factored loads at the service limit state. The static resistance along the shaft and at the toe can be estimated from laboratory shear strength parameters, in-situ test data (SPT, CPT), or geomaterial parameters back-analysed from performance data.
key_points: Four static analyses: axial compression, axial tension, lateral resistance and deformation, pile group settlement
Factored resistance = smaller of the factored geotechnical resistance and the factored structural resistance
Settlement and lateral deformation of groups use factored loads at the service limit state

subsections.title: Events During and After Pile Driving
subsections.body: The soil and weaker rock in which a pile is installed are almost always disturbed (p. 214). The degree of disturbance depends on the soil and rock type and density, the pile type (displacement or low-displacement) and the installation method (driven, vibrated, drilled, jetted); for driven piles substantial disturbance and remolding is unavoidable. Over the long term, scour, settlement, pore pressure fluctuations, seismic and other extreme events may occur, and are addressed in the strength, extreme event and service limit states so that the embedment and foundation stiffness are sufficient.

subsections.title: Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: The resistance of piles driven into cohesionless soil depends primarily on the relative density of the soil (pp. 214-216). Driving increases the relative density of loose to medium dense soil close to the pile through vibration and lateral displacement, most of all next to displacement piles; Broms (1966) and later studies found the zone of densification extends 3 to 5.5 diameters from the pile shaft and 3 to 5 diameters below the pile toe (Figure 7-1). Large-displacement piles such as closed-end pipe and precast concrete piles densify cohesionless soil more than low-displacement open-end pipe or steel H-piles. In dense sands and gravels, negative pore pressures generated during driving can temporarily increase the resistance; as they dissipate the resistance decreases (relaxation), as the shear strength equation shows (Eq. 7-1). In saturated cohesionless silts and loose to medium dense fine sands, driving can generate high positive pore pressures that temporarily reduce the resistance; the gain with time (setup) is generally quicker than in clays because pore pressures dissipate faster.

subsections.title: Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: When piles are driven into saturated cohesive soil, the soil near the pile is disturbed and radially compressed (pp. 216-217). In soft or normally consolidated clays the zone of disturbance is generally within one pile diameter around the pile; in saturated stiff clays there are also changes in secondary structure (closing of fissures), remolding and loss of previous stress history effects next to the pile. Figure 7-2 (after Broms 1966) shows the disturbance zone and the heave that displacement piles can cause. The disturbance generates high excess positive pore pressures that temporarily reduce the shear strength, the nominal geotechnical resistance and the blow count; as the soil reconsolidates, the shear strength and resistance increase (setup), the opposite of relaxation. The zone and magnitude of disturbance depend on the soil sensitivity, the driving method and the pile geometry. Limited data for partially saturated cohesive soils indicate that driving does not generate high pore pressures, so significant setup does not occur.
figures: Figure 7-2: Disturbance of cohesive soils during pile driving (after Broms 1966)

subsections.title: Additional Soil Resistance Considerations
subsections.body: Many projects need more than one static analysis (pp. 217-219): one for the number and length of piles to support the structure loads, and a second for the resistance the pile will meet during installation, which sets the capability of the driving equipment and the minimum pile section for drivability. At a bridge pier subject to scour (Figure 7-3) the first analysis neglects the soil in the scour zone, which may not be available for long-term support, and the second includes it because it resists driving; piles driven through loose uncompacted fill (Figure 7-4) are treated the same way. The resistance computed in the scourable or unsuitable layer is added to the required nominal resistance to give the required nominal driving resistance. The plans should give the controlling factored load, the nominal resistance, the required nominal driving resistance and the minimum penetration depth: in the manual's example 420 kips of soil resistance must be overcome to reach the minimum penetration for a 300-kip nominal resistance in compression, and specifying only the 300 kips could be misinterpreted and lead to claims (driving criteria: Chapter 17).

subsections.title: Load Transfer
subsections.body: The nominal resistance Rn of a pile in homogeneous soil is the sum of the shaft resistance Rs and the toe resistance Rp (Eq. 7-2, p. 219). The equation assumes the pile toe and shaft have both moved enough relative to the adjacent soil to develop the nominal shaft and toe resistances at the same time; generally the displacement needed to mobilize the shaft resistance is smaller than that needed for the toe. This approach has been used for all piles except very large piles, more than 36 inches in diameter or width. Figure 7-5 shows typical load transfer profiles, as obtained from a static load test with strain gages or telltales along the shaft: (a) no shaft resistance, the full head load reaching the toe; (b) uniform shaft resistance, typical of cohesive soil; (c) triangular shaft resistance, typical of cohesionless soil.
equations: Eq. 7-2: Rn = Rs + Rp

subsections.title: Effective Stress
subsections.body: The vertical effective stress at a depth is the total vertical stress from the weight of the overlying soil minus the pore water pressure there (pp. 221-222). An Effective Stress Diagram plots it against depth and is used in many static resistance and settlement calculations. It needs the total unit weight and thickness of each layer (from the boring logs, density tests on undisturbed cohesive samples, or SPT N values with the visual classification) and the depth of the water table; the total vertical stress is summed layer by layer (Section 5.2.2) and the pore pressure is the unit weight of water (62.4 lb/ft3) times the height of water. The design water table should be compared with the levels found in the subsurface exploration and allow for seasonal variation. Figures 7-6 and 7-7 are examples with the water table below and above the ground surface.

subsections.title: Resistance Factors
subsections.body: Resistance factors for driven pile design are in AASHTO (2014) Table 10.6.5.2.3-1 (pp. 223-226). A resistance factor is a statistically based multiplier on the nominal resistance from a specific analysis method, tied with the load factors to a target reliability index beta; it is not a direct replacement for an allowable stress design factor of safety. With a static analysis the factored resistance Rr is at most the shaft resistance times the shaft method's resistance factor plus the toe resistance times the toe method's factor (Eq. 7-3), with Rs = fs As and Rp = qp Ap (Eqs. 7-4, 7-5). Table 7-1 gives the static analysis factors: compression - alpha-method 0.35, Schmertmann (1975) 0.50, Nordlund 0.45, the beta-method differing between AASHTO and the manual, Brown (2001), API RP2A and Eslami and Fellenius not in AASHTO; block failure in cohesive soil 0.60; tension - Nordlund 0.35, alpha 0.25, beta 0.20, lambda 0.30, SPT 0.25, CPT 0.40; group uplift 0.50; lateral 1.0. Where the nominal resistance is found by a static load test, dynamic testing, wave equation analysis or a dynamic formula, the field method's factor phi_dyn is used (Table 7-2): 0.80 for a static load test with dynamic testing, 0.75 for a static load test alone or dynamic testing of every production pile, 0.65 for dynamic testing of at least two piles per site condition and 2 % of production piles, 0.50 for the wave equation at end of drive, 0.40 for the FHWA Modified Gates formula, 0.10 for the Engineering News formula; in tension 0.60 for a static load test and 0.50 for dynamic testing with signal matching. For a small group (fewer than 3 piles per substructure unit in this manual) AASHTO recommends reducing the factors in Tables 7-1 and 7-2 by 20 %. The AASHTO calibration considered few large diameter pipe piles (Brown and Thompson 2015), which a designer of piles over 24 inches should consider.

subsections.title: Interdiscipline Communication and Coordination
subsections.body: Design and construction need clear communication among the structural, geotechnical, geologic, hydraulic and construction professionals (p. 227). Figure 2-3 in Chapter 2 gives the flow chart of the driven pile design and construction process with the main areas of coordination in LRFD design and construction, and Tables 2-4 and 2-5 detail what is communicated. Effective communication is essential to a cost-effective foundation that meets all the strength, extreme event and service limit state requirements.

sections.title: Strength Limit States
sections.summary: Geotechnical strength checks: axial compression and uplift of single piles and groups, bearing stratum punching, and drivability. Seven static methods for piles in soil (7.2.1.3): Nordlund, alpha, API RP2A, effective stress beta, Brown (SPT), Eslami and Fellenius (CPT), Nottingham and Schmertmann (CPT); piles in soft rock and to hard rock (7.2.1.4). FHWA recommends Nordlund for cohesionless soils, alpha for cohesive soils, and API for large diameter pipe piles. Also: group compression, tension, setup and relaxation, lateral resistance, length estimates, groundwater, dewatering, scour, downdrag.
sections.body: 7.2 Strength Limit States (p. 227). The strength limit state ensures local and global strength and stability against statistically significant load combinations occurring during the structure design life. Strength limit state design includes an evaluation of the nominal geotechnical and structural resistances, as well as the loss of lateral and vertical support in the design flood event due to scour. Geotechnical aspects of strength limit state design include: axial compression resistance of single piles; axial compression resistance of pile groups; uplift resistance of single piles; uplift resistance of pile groups; bearing stratum punching failure; and constructability, including drivability. Subsections: 7.2.1 Determination of Nominal Resistance for Single Piles; 7.2.2 Resistance of Pile Groups in Axial Compression; 7.2.3 Design for Axial Tension Resistance; 7.2.4 Nominal Axial Resistance Changes after Pile Driving; 7.2.5 Nominal Lateral Resistance; 7.2.6 Pile Length Estimates for Contract Documents; 7.2.7 Groundwater Effects and Buoyancy; 7.2.8 Site Dewatering; 7.2.9 Scour; 7.2.10 Downdrag.

subsections.title: Determination of Nominal Resistance for Single Piles
subsections.body: Static analysis methods for the nominal axial resistance of a single driven pile (printed pp. 227-278): the general approach (7.2.1.1), an overview of the methods and when each applies (7.2.1.2), seven methods for piles in soil (7.2.1.3: Nordlund, alpha, P2A/API, effective stress beta, Brown, Eslami and Fellenius, Nottingham and Schmertmann), piles to soft and weak or hard rock (7.2.1.4), and software for the computations (7.2.1.5). The FHWA recommended methods are Nordlund in cohesionless soils, the alpha-method in cohesive soils and the API method for large diameter pipe piles.

subsections.title: General
subsections.body: Numerous static analysis methods are available for the nominal geotechnical resistance of a single pile (printed pp. 227-229). Section 7.2.1.3 details methods for piles in cohesionless, cohesive and layered profiles from SPT or laboratory data, and methods based on CPT results. A method should have proven agreement with full-scale field results in soil conditions like the project's, with the pile type and installation conditions (impact or vibratory driving) to be used, and some AASHTO resistance factors require specific procedures for the soil strength properties. A static analysis iteratively assumes a pile depth. Regional geology or construction control may justify local calibration of methods and resistance factors. Table 7-3 compares the methods in AASHTO (2014) with those in the manual: Meyerhof (1976, SPT) 0.30, Nordlund 0.45, alpha-method 0.35, beta-method (AASHTO) 0.25, lambda-method 0.40 and Schmertmann (1975, CPT) 0.50 have AASHTO resistance factors; API RP2A, Brown (2001) and Eslami and Fellenius (1997) have none; the manual's beta-method follows Fellenius (1991) and differs from AASHTO's.

subsections.title: Static Analysis Overview
subsections.body: Agencies often specify design methods based on experience; the methods in this chapter should be chosen by their applicability to the soil conditions, the pile type and the laboratory or in-situ data (printed pp. 229-232). Tables 7-4 and 7-5 give an overview of methods for cohesionless and cohesive soils; in layered profiles the applicable method is used in each layer, and Table 7-3 identifies methods for mixed profiles and the CPT methods. Static analyses typically estimate the pile length for a given nominal resistance to set the contract quantities; the lengths and resistance are then confirmed during construction by a field resistance determination method and a driving criterion (Chapter 17). Where static analysis alone is the resistance determination method and piles are driven to a predetermined toe elevation, the design pile lengths must address site variability. The FHWA recommended methods are the Nordlund method in cohesionless soils (7.2.1.3.1), the alpha-method in cohesive soils (7.2.1.3.2) and the API method for large diameter pipe piles (7.2.1.3.3), based on FHWA experience with their reliability for conventional pile types.

subsections.title: Nordlund Method (Cohesionless Soils)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.1 Nordlund Method - Cohesionless Soils (pp. 232-245). The Nordlund Method (1963) is based on field observations and considers the shape of pile taper and its soil displacement in calculating the shaft resistance. It also accounts for the differences in soil-pile coefficient of friction for different pile materials, and is based on load test programs in cohesionless soils with timber, H, closed end pipe, Monotube and Raymond step taper piles, generally 10 to 20 inches wide. Large diameter open end pipe piles, concrete cylinder piles, 24 inch and greater square prestressed concrete piles and 16 and 18 inch H-pile sections are not in the calibration database; the method tends to over predict the nominal resistance for pile widths larger than 24 inches, and alternative static analysis methods should be evaluated for these pile types and sizes. The shaft resistance is a function of the friction angle of the soil, the friction angle on the sliding surface, the pile taper, the effective unit weight of the soil, the pile length, the minimum pile perimeter and the volume of soil displaced (Figure 7-8, Eq. 7-6); for a pile of uniform cross section (omega = 0) in layers of the same effective unit weight and friction angle it becomes Eq. 7-7. The soil friction angle phi influences most of the calculations; without laboratory data it can be estimated from corrected SPT N values (Section 5.2.3). Figures 7-8 to 7-14 give the design parameters, and Tables 7-6 and 7-7 give the coefficient of lateral earth pressure. Nordlund placed no limiting value on the shaft resistance but recommended that the vertical effective stress at the pile toe used for the toe resistance be limited to 3 ksf. Procedure (Steps 1-6 shaft, 7-9 toe): (1) delineate the soil profile into layers and determine phi for each (effective stress diagram, Section 7.1.4; corrected SPT N values (N1)60, Section 5.1.1; phi from Table 5-5 without laboratory or in-situ data); (2) delta from the displaced soil volume per unit length V and phi, using the delta/phi ratio for the pile type from Figure 7-9; (3) K_delta for V and the taper angle omega from Figures 7-10 to 7-13, interpolating linearly on phi and log-linearly on V between the 0.1, 1.0 and 10.0 ft3/ft curves (Tables 7-6 and 7-7 give interpolated values for uniform piles, omega = 0); (4) the correction factor C_F from Figure 7-14 with phi and delta/phi; (5) the average vertical effective stress at the midpoint of each layer (no limiting value); (6) the shaft resistance of each layer by Eq. 7-8, summed to Rs, using the 'box' area for H-piles (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (7) alpha_t from Figure 7-16(a) for the pile length to diameter ratio and N'q from Figure 7-16(b), with phi near the toe (from SPT data, the average (N1)60 from the toe to 3 diameters below it); (8) the vertical effective stress at the toe, limited to 3 ksf; (9) Rp by Eq. 7-9, limited to qL Ap with qL from Figure 7-15, using the lesser value; for steel H and open end pipe piles the toe area (steel only, or steel and enclosed soil) is chosen from past experience and local correlations with static load tests; (10) Rn = Rs + Rp; (11) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (0.45 in sand); the factor of the field verification method, phi_dyn (Table 7-2), may also be used.

subsections.title: Alpha Method (Cohesive Soils)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.2 alpha-Method - Cohesive Soils (pp. 245-251). For piles in clay a total stress analysis is often used, with the nominal resistance calculated from the undrained shear strength. It assumes the shaft resistance is independent of the vertical effective stress and the unit shaft resistance is an empirical adhesion factor times the undrained shear strength. The unit shaft resistance equals the adhesion, the shear stress between the pile surface and the soil at failure (Eq. 7-10). The adhesion factor alpha depends on the nature and strength of the clay, pile dimension, method of installation and time effects; it varies within wide limits and decreases rapidly with increasing shear strength. Figure 7-17 should generally be used for adhesion, unless one of the special soil stratigraphy cases of Figure 7-18 is present; where either could be used, the inexperienced user should take the smaller value. The charts cover undrained shear strengths from about 0.5 ksf to 3.5 to 5.0 ksf, depending on the chart; users should confirm a chart's applicability with local correlations between static resistance calculations and static load tests, particularly near its limits. Figure 7-17 gives the pile adhesion Ca against su by pile type and embedded length to diameter ratio D/b, D being the lesser of the length from the ground surface to the bottom of the clay layer or to the pile toe. Figure 7-18 gives alpha against su for unique stratigraphy and embedment, used only for the adhesion of a stiff clay layer in that condition (clay layers of different consistency each get their own alpha): the top graph for piles driven through sand or sandy gravel into stiff clay (the highest alpha, falling with penetration into the clay), the middle graph for soft clay over stiff clay (alpha rising with penetration into the stiff clay), the bottom graph for stiff clay without different overlying strata (a gap forms along the upper shaft, so alpha is reduced at shallow penetration). In highly overconsolidated clays where su exceeds the upper limits of Figures 7-17 and 7-18, alpha is calculated by API Recommended Practice 2A (1993), Section 7.2.1.3.3. For H-piles in cohesive soils the shaft resistance is taken on the 'box' area: Ca on the exterior flange area plus su on the two remaining sides, approximated by the corrugated pile curve of Figure 7-17 times the box area (Section 7.10.7). In clays with large shrink-swell potential the adhesion in the shrink-swell zone is ignored. The unit toe resistance is qp = Nc su (Eq. 7-11), Nc usually taken as 9 for deep foundations. On smaller piles the toe resistance is a low percentage of the nominal resistance and is sometimes ignored; on larger piles the movement to mobilize the toe resistance is several times that for the shaft, by which the shaft resistance may have dropped to a residual value. Procedure: (1) delineate layers and determine Ca from Figure 7-17 or alpha from Figure 7-18 for each, with su, D and b (Section 7.2.1.3.3 where su exceeds the charts); (2) fs by Eq. 7-10; (3) the shaft resistance of each layer, summed to Rs; (4) qp by Eq. 7-11; (5) Rp (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (0.35); phi_dyn of the field verification method (Table 7-2) may also be used.

subsections.title: P2A (API RP2A) Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.3 API Method - Mixed Soil Profiles (pp. 251-255; the heading is printed 'P2A Method'). The American Petroleum Institute static analysis procedure was developed for offshore construction, which almost exclusively uses large diameter open end steel pipe piles driven by impact hammer to final penetration (API 1993). NCHRP Report 20-05 (Brown and Thompson 2015) defines large diameter open end pipe piles as 36 inches in diameter or greater, steel pipe or concrete cylinder piles; their use on transportation projects has increased significantly. Cohesive soil: the unit shaft resistance is fs = alpha su (Eq. 7-12), alpha from psi = su/sigma'vo by Eqs. 7-13 to 7-15. An alpha of 1.0 is recommended for unconsolidated clays; for very long piles, where residual strengths are approached through extended driving and soil displacement, API (1993) recommends engineering judgment. The unit toe resistance is qp = 9 su (Eq. 7-16). The pile may be unplugged during driving but plugged under static loads; both cases should be considered in the static analysis and drivability study. Cohesionless soil: fs = K_delta sigma'vo tan(delta) (Eq. 7-17), with K_delta = 0.8 for tension and compression of unplugged open end pipe piles and 1.0 for the plugged or closed end case (API 1993); qp = sigma'vo Nq (Eq. 7-18). Table 7-8 (modified from API 1993) gives the soil-pile friction angle, limiting unit shaft resistance, Nq and limiting unit toe resistance for steel pipe piles in cohesionless siliceous soil; site exploration and testing data should be used in lieu of these guidelines where necessary. Procedure: (1) cohesive layers: average su and sigma'vo at mid-layer, alpha from su/sigma'vo by Eq. 7-13 or 7-14; cohesionless layers: delta, sigma'vo at mid-layer and K_delta from the pile type and loading direction; (2) fs by Eq. 7-12 in cohesive layers or Eq. 7-17 in cohesionless layers (with the limiting unit shaft resistance); (3) Rs by Eq. 7-4; (4) qp by Eq. 7-16 for a toe in a cohesive layer, or Nq from Table 7-8 and Eq. 7-18 in a cohesionless layer (with the limiting unit toe resistance); (5) Rp by Eq. 7-5 (Section 7.10.7 on plugging); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance with the factor of the field verification method. Paikowsky (2004, NCHRP Report 507) evaluated the method's reliability in cohesive soils but not in sands or mixed profiles, and AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for it, so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.

subsections.title: Effective Stress Methods
subsections.body: Sections 7.2.1.3.4 to 7.2.1.3.7 (pp. 255-268) give four further static analysis methods for single piles in soil: the effective stress beta-method for mixed soil profiles (7.2.1.3.4), the Brown method for mixed soil profiles from SPT data (7.2.1.3.5), and two methods from CPT data, Eslami and Fellenius (7.2.1.3.6) and Nottingham and Schmertmann (7.2.1.3.7).

subsections.title: Beta Method (Effective Stress)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.4 Effective Stress beta-Method - Mixed Soil Profiles (pp. 255-258). Static resistance in cohesionless, cohesive and layered soils can also be calculated by an effective stress method, developed to model the long term drained shear strength conditions; the effective stress friction angle phi' is used in parameter selection. The unit shaft resistance is fs = beta sigma'vo (Eq. 7-19), beta being the Bjerrum-Burland coefficient K_delta tan(delta); the unit toe resistance is qp = Nt sigma'p (Eq. 7-20). Table 7-9 gives Fellenius's (2014) recommended ranges of beta and Nt by soil type and phi'. Fellenius notes that the factors affecting beta and Nt include the soil composition (grain size distribution, angularity and mineralogical origin of the grains), the original soil density and the density due to pile installation, and the soil strength; values can deviate significantly from the table, and beta seldom exceeds 1.0. For sedimentary cohesionless deposits Nt ranges from about 30 to 120; in very dense deposits such as glacial tills it can be much higher but can also approach 30. In clays an Nt of 3 gives a toe resistance similar to a traditional undrained analysis, so a relatively low Nt is recommended in clays unless local correlations suggest higher values. Selected coefficients should be confirmed with local correlations between static resistance calculations and load tests. The method places no limiting values on the shaft or toe resistance. Procedure: (1) layers and phi' (effective stress diagram, Section 7.1.4; sigma'vo at the midpoint of each layer; phi' from laboratory or in-situ data, or for cohesionless layers from (N1)60 by a method in Section 5.2.3); (2) beta from local experience or Table 7-9; (3) fs by Eq. 7-19; (4) the shaft resistance of each layer, summed to Rs (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (5) qp by Eq. 7-20, Nt from local experience or Table 7-9 and sigma'p at the toe; (6) Rp by Eq. 7-5; (7) Rn = Rs + Rp; (8) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for the beta-method by Fellenius (Table 7-1: the AASHTO beta-method is based on Skempton), so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.
key_points: Effective stress method for cohesionless, cohesive and layered soils, modelling long term drained conditions with phi'

subsections.title: Brown Method (SPT N60)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.5 Brown Method - Mixed Soil Profiles - SPT Data (pp. 258-260). The Brown Method (2001) is a simple empirical method using SPT N60 values for the unit shaft and unit toe resistance, based on correlations with 71 static load tests from Caltrans projects in a wide variety of soil types, with closed end pipe, open end pipe, H-piles and precast concrete piles; it considers compression and uplift loading and the installation method (impact driving and partial vibratory installation). The average unit shaft resistance is fs = Fvs (Ab + Bb N60) (Eq. 7-21), with N60 taken as 50 if greater than 50 and as 3 if less than 3. Brown recommended the shaft resistance be the unit shaft resistance times the 'box' perimeter for H-piles rather than the actual pile/soil contact area, and only the external surface area for open end pipe piles. Ab, Bb and Fvs are given in Table 7-10. For impact driven piles qp = 3.55 N60 (Eq. 7-22), multiplied by 0.56 for vibratory installed piles; Rp = qp (Ap + App Fp) (Eq. 7-23), Ap being the actual steel area at the toe for H-piles and open end pipe piles. The method is recommended only for preliminary length estimates until a greater experience base exists; Caltrans continues to study and expand it (Olson and Shantz 2004). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for it, so the factor of the applicable field verification method, phi_dyn, should be used.
key_points: Empirical SPT N60 method from 71 Caltrans static load tests in a wide variety of soils (closed and open end pipe, H and precast concrete piles; compression and uplift)

Shaft area: 'box' perimeter for H-piles; external surface only for open end pipe piles

subsections.title: Eslami and Fellenius CPT Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.6 Eslami and Fellenius Method - CPT Data (pp. 260-262). The unit shaft resistance is correlated to the average effective cone tip resistance, with a shaft correlation coefficient applied based on the soil profile: fs = Cs qE (Eq. 7-24), with the Eslami cone stress qE = qt - U2 (Eq. 7-25) and qt = qc + U2 (1 - a) (Eq. 7-26); Cs is given by soil type in Table 7-11 (after Fellenius 2014). The unit toe resistance qp = Cp qEg (Eq. 7-27) uses the geometric average of the cone tip resistance over the influence zone at the pile toe, after correction for pore pressure on the cone shoulder and for effective stress. The zone of influence depends on the pile diameter b: from 4b below to 8b above the toe when the pile is installed through a weak zone overlying a dense zone, and from 4b below to 2b above the toe when it is driven through a dense soil into a weak soil. The toe correction coefficient Cp is 1.0 in most cases; because larger piles need more movement to mobilize the toe resistance, Cp = 12/b (b in inches) for pile diameters greater than 16 inches (Eq. 7-28). Procedure: (1) obtain CPT results with cone stress and pore pressure measurements; (2) fs for each depth increment by Eq. 7-24 with Table 7-11; (3) the shaft resistance of each layer and Rs by Eq. 7-4; (4) qp by Eq. 7-27; (5) Rp by Eq. 7-5; (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for this method, so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.

subsections.title: Nottingham and Schmertmann CPT Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.7 Nottingham and Schmertmann Method - CPT Data (pp. 262-268). An empirical procedure used in U.S. practice, from Nottingham and Schmertmann (1975) as summarized in FHWA-TS-78-209, 'Guidelines for Cone Penetration Test, Performance and Design' (Schmertmann 1978). In cohesionless soils the nominal shaft resistance is derived from the CPT unit sleeve friction (Eq. 7-29), Ks being the ratio of unit pile shaft resistance to unit cone sleeve friction as a function of the full penetration depth D, with the sleeve friction averaged over 0 to 8b and 8b to D. The transfer function Ks varies with total penetration (depth of embedment / pile diameter), pile material and cone type; no limit was imposed on sleeve friction in the original procedure. Without sleeve friction data, Rs = Cf sum(qc As) (Eq. 7-30), Cf from Table 7-12. In cohesive soils Rs = alpha' fs As (Eq. 7-31), alpha' being the ratio of pile shaft resistance to cone sleeve friction, patterned after Tomlinson's alpha-method, which varies with fs as shown in Figure 7-20; the method is expected to be less appropriate in sensitive soils, where the friction sleeve meets severely disturbed soil behind the cone tip. The toe resistance (Figure 7-21) uses an averaging scheme over 8 pile diameters above to as much as 3.75 diameters below the toe, favoring the lower qc values; the authors refer to a 'limit' qc of 105 to 315 ksf applied to qp unless local experience warrants higher values, and with mechanical cone soundings in cohesive soils qp is reduced by 40 percent for toe resistance effects on the base of the friction sleeve. Soil plugging (Section 7.10.7) needs careful consideration in choosing the toe area of low displacement open ended pipe and H-piles. Procedure: (1) delineate layers from qc and fs; (2) the shaft resistance of each layer: in cohesionless soils from the layer's average fs and K, with K from Figure 7-19 for the full pile penetration depth to diameter ratio (not the layer's), d being the toe depth or the depth to the bottom of the layer, whichever is less, the 'box' area for H-piles, Eq. 7-32 below a depth of 8b, and Eq. 7-30 without sleeve friction data; in cohesive soils Eq. 7-31; (3) Rs as the sum of the layers; (4) qp by Eq. 7-33; (5) Rp, using only the steel area at the toe of steel H and unfilled open end pipe piles unless there is reasonable assurance and experience that a plug will form (then the 'box' area or the full pipe area); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (Schmertmann 1975, 0.50); phi_dyn (Table 7-2) may also be used. Under Eq. 7-29 (p. 263) the print takes Ks from Figure 7-20; Step 2a and Eq. 7-32 take it from Figure 7-19, the sand curves.

subsections.title: Nominal Axial Resistance from Rock
subsections.body: For piles driven to rock, the nominal toe resistance on rock is typically controlled by the structural capacity of the pile section rather than the rock strength. The geotechnical toe resistance in rock can be estimated from the uniaxial compressive strength. For very hard rock, the pile structural resistance controls.
key_points: Rock toe resistance often controlled by pile structural capacity, not rock strength

Must verify pile can be driven to rock without damage (drivability check)

subsections.title: Software for Single Pile Nominal Resistance Computations
subsections.body: FHWA previously sponsored the DRIVEN program, which used the FHWA recommended Nordlund and alpha-methods (printed pp. 274-278). The public domain version is no longer available from FHWA; a commercial version, DrivenPiles, was released in 2015. Table 7-15 lists the static analysis methods in commercially available programs (AllPile, A-Pile, DrivenPiles, FB-Deep, Unipile), alphabetically; FHWA endorses no program. An example soil profile (Figure 7-23) is analysed with DRIVEN using the FHWA method (Figure 7-24), APILE using the Nordlund and alpha methods (Figure 7-25) and UNIPILE using the beta-method (Figure 7-26). DRIVEN and APILE, though both using the FHWA method, differ by about 10 % in toe and nominal resistance at the final 125 ft penetration and at layer transitions, because APILE averages the toe resistance around layer transitions; UNIPILE, using effective stresses in all layers, gives a lower resistance.

subsections.title: Pile Groups in Compression
subsections.body: Discusses the behavior and capacity of pile groups under axial compression loads. Group capacity may be controlled by the sum of individual pile capacities (modified by group efficiency) or by block failure of the group acting as a unit. The group efficiency factor accounts for interaction effects when piles are closely spaced. AASHTO (2014) requires evaluation of both individual and block failure modes.

AASHTO phi for group = 0.65 (individual) or method-specific phi (block failure)

Block failure mode critical for cohesive soils at close spacing

For cohesionless soils, group efficiency typically >= 1.0 at typical spacings (3B c/c)
Minimum spacing 2.5B or 30 inches per AASHTO; 3B preferred

subsections.title: Pile Group Efficiency
subsections.body: Group efficiency factor Eg reduces the sum of individual pile resistances to account for interaction. Converse-Labarre formula (Eq 7-35) is the standard approach.

subsections.title: Block Failure in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: For closely spaced piles in cohesive soils, the group may fail as a block with shaft resistance on the perimeter and base bearing on the group footprint area.

subsections.title: Block Failure in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: Block failure in cohesionless soils uses perimeter shaft resistance and base bearing capacity on the group footprint. This mode is rarely critical for typical spacings.

subsections.title: Design for Axial Tension Resistance
subsections.body: Uplift resistance has become increasingly important for structures subject to seismic loading and in some cases sets the minimum pile penetration, where an axial tension load test can pay for itself through its higher resistance factor (printed p. 288; procedures in Kyfor et al. 1992 and Chapter 9). The factored uplift resistance of a single pile is the nominal shaft resistance from an AASHTO static analysis method times the uplift resistance factor phi_up (Eq. 7-38). A pile group's uplift resistance is the lesser of the sum of the individual pile resistances in tension and the resistance of the group as a block (Eqs. 7-39 to 7-41).

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Single Piles
subsections.body: In fine grained cohesive soils loaded undrained the shaft resistance is generally taken as equal in compression and uplift (De Nicola and Randolph 1993) (printed pp. 288-290). In free-draining soils it has been customary to take the uplift shaft resistance as about 70 % of the compression shaft resistance, and De Nicola and Randolph concluded piles have lower uplift than compression shaft resistance; API (1993) and a case reported by Altaee et al. (1992) take them as about equal. Under cyclic or sustained uplift the resistance can fall from a peak to a residual value in clays, and particle degradation can reduce it in sands (Tomlinson 1994). The factored uplift resistance is the nominal shaft resistance from any AASHTO static analysis method times phi_up from Table 7-1 (Eq. 7-38); per AASHTO Article C10.7.3.10 phi_up is 80 % of the compression shaft factor, so the shaft resistance is not reduced further. With a tension static load test an uplift resistance factor up to 0.60 may be used, and with dynamic tests with signal matching up to 0.50. Figure 7-32 is a design chart for uplift loading computed with the FHWA method (Nordlund / alpha-method) in APILE.
equations: Eq. 7-38: Rr = phi Rn = phi_up Rs
figures: Figure 7-32: Design chart for nominal and factored resistance in axial tension

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Pile Groups
subsections.body: Group uplift resistance often sets the minimum pile penetration and can control the design, for example under cofferdam seals with large buoyancy forces, cantilever segmental construction, and seismic, vessel impact or debris loading, or where piles in tension are driven to a shallow bearing stratum (printed pp. 290-293). AASHTO (2014) limits the group uplift resistance to the lesser of the sum of the individual pile resistances in tension and the resistance of the group as a block; its specifications are considered relatively conservative, particularly in cohesionless soils. The factored group resistance is phi_ug Rug with phi_ug = 0.50 (Eq. 7-39). The printed contents number the two subsections that follow 7.2.3.2.1 and 7.2.3.2.2; the headings in the text, used here, number them 7.2.3.2.2 and 7.2.3.2.3.
equations: Eq. 7-39: Rr = phi Rn = phi_ug Rug

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Groups in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: In cohesionless soils AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.11 limits the nominal group resistance in tension to the lesser of two resistances (printed pp. 291-292): the sum of the individual pile nominal shaft resistances times the uplift resistance factor of the analysis method times the number of piles (Eq. 7-40), and the effective weight of the block of soil extending upward from the pile toe level at a slope of 1H:4V (Tomlinson 1994; Figure 7-33), the weight of the piles in the block taken as equal to the weight of soil. (Printed contents: 7.2.3.2.1.)
equations: Eq. 7-40: Rr = phi Rug = phi_up Rs n
figures: Figure 7-33: Uplift of pile group in cohesionless soil (after Tomlinson 1994)

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Groups in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: In cohesive soils AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.11 limits the nominal group uplift resistance to the lesser of Eq. 7-40 and Eq. 7-41, the block resistance from the weight of the pile/soil block including the pile cap and the undrained shear resistance along the group perimeter (printed pp. 292-293; Figure 7-34): Rug = 2D(B + Z)su + Wg, with D the embedded pile length, B and Z the group width and length, su the weighted average undrained shear strength over the embedded depth along the group perimeter, and Wg the effective weight of the pile/soil block including the cap. (Printed contents: 7.2.3.2.2.)
equations: Eq. 7-41: Rn = Rug = 2D(B + Z)su + Wg
figures: Figure 7-34: Uplift of pile group in cohesive soils (after Tomlinson 1994)

subsections.title: Resistance Changes After Driving
subsections.body: This section covers time-dependent changes in pile resistance after driving, including relaxation (resistance decrease) and soil setup (resistance increase). These phenomena significantly affect the relationship between driving resistance and long-term static capacity.
key_points: Relaxation: resistance decreases over time after driving (primarily toe resistance in dense fine-grained soils)
Setup: resistance increases over time as excess pore pressures dissipate (primarily shaft resistance in clays)
Setup factor = R_n(t)/R_n(EOD); ranges from 1.2 in sands to 5.5+ in sensitive clays
Setup primarily affects shaft resistance in clays; may take days to years
Relaxation most common in dense silts, shales, and weathered rock
AASHTO requires restrike testing when setup or relaxation is expected
Pore pressure estimation during driving from Eq 7-47 and Figure 7-35
equations: Eq 7-42: R_setup = R_n(t) / R_n(EOD) (setup factor definition)
Eq 7-43: R_n(t) = R_n(EOD) * [1 + A * log10(t/t_EOD)] (Skov and Denver 1988 setup equation)
Eq 7-44: A = setup rate parameter (0.2 for sand, 0.6 for clay, Table 7-16)
Eq 7-45: R_setup = (Q_t - Q_EOD) / Q_EOD (measured setup from restrike)
Eq 7-46: R_n_design = R_n(EOD) + phi_setup * R_setup (design resistance including setup)
Eq 7-47: Delta_u / sigma'_v0 = (sigma'_v0 + Delta_sigma_v) * A_f - sigma'_v0 (pore pressure from driving)

subsections.title: Relaxation
subsections.body: Relaxation is a decrease in pile resistance over time after driving. It is most commonly observed in dense silts, shales, and weathered rock where driving generates negative pore pressures that temporarily increase effective stresses. As the negative pore pressures dissipate, resistance decreases.

subsections.title: Soil Setup
subsections.body: Soil setup is the increase in pile resistance over time, primarily due to dissipation of excess positive pore water pressures generated during driving in cohesive soils. The rate and magnitude depend on soil type, sensitivity, permeability, and pile type.

subsections.title: Design Considerations for Setup and Relaxation
subsections.body: Designers must determine whether to rely on setup or account for relaxation. Setup can be incorporated using the Skov-Denver equation with appropriate resistance factors. Restrike testing is required to verify assumed setup values.

subsections.title: Nominal Lateral Resistance
subsections.body: The nominal lateral resistance of driven piles is typically evaluated using p-y analysis methods as detailed in Section 7.3.7. For the strength limit state, the structural capacity of the pile under combined axial and lateral loading must be checked.
key_points: Lateral resistance evaluation uses p-y methods (detailed in Section 7.3.7)
Strength limit state requires structural check under combined loading
Refer to Chapter 8 for structural design of piles

subsections.title: Pile Length Estimates for Contract Documents
subsections.body: Discusses procedures for estimating pile lengths for contract documents based on static analysis results. Estimated lengths should be consistent with the required factored resistance and the subsurface conditions at each substructure location.
key_points: Estimated pile lengths based on static analysis required for plans and specifications
Order lengths should include contingency for subsurface variability
Pile length estimates should consider setup/relaxation effects

subsections.title: Groundwater Effects and Buoyancy
subsections.body: The nominal resistance in axial compression and tension and the lateral resistance can change with the groundwater elevation through the resulting change in vertical effective stress (printed p. 302). Droughts, regional construction such as tunnels, or local excavation dewatering can lower the groundwater; a temporary lowering increases the effective stress on the pile, so a pile driven to the required nominal resistance under it will have less than the required resistance when the groundwater returns to its normal elevation. Buoyant forces should also be considered: a closed-end pipe pile driven through soft soils to rock or a hard bearing layer may need a thicker wall or other measures, since buoyancy can raise a sealed closed-end pile off the bearing layer if the shaft resistance alone cannot resist it.
key_points: A temporarily lowered water table increases effective stress: piles driven then lose resistance when it recovers
Buoyancy can lift a sealed closed-end pipe pile off its bearing layer if the shaft resistance is insufficient

subsections.title: Site Dewatering
subsections.body: Dewatering a site during construction temporarily increases the effective stresses and the soil shear strength, so piles develop more resistance at a shallower penetration and the soil resistance to reach a specified depth is greater (printed pp. 302-303); a pile type not checked for this may not be drivable to the required depth. When dewatering stops the water table rises, the effective stresses and shear strength fall, and piles driven to the nominal resistance in the dewatered condition have less than the required nominal resistance. Where significant dewatering is needed, multiple static analyses should give the nominal resistance and drivability in the short-term dewatered condition and the long-term nominal resistance afterwards. Dewatering can also increase the drag force on nearby deep foundations or cause consolidation settlement of nearby structures, which should be evaluated in design.
key_points: Dewatering raises resistance during driving and lowers it once the water table recovers
Analyse both the dewatered (driving) and the long-term condition
Check effects on adjacent structures: drag force and consolidation settlement
subsections.applicability: Driven pile sites dewatered during construction, and structures near them.

subsections.title: Artesian Conditions
subsections.body: Artesian conditions develop where a permeable layer or aquifer is confined between two impermeable layers and outcrops at an elevation higher than where it is met in-situ; the effective stresses on the pile then depend directly on the head of water (printed p. 303). They can give lower than expected nominal resistance in the layer and vertical groundwater migration along the pile-soil interface; Harris et al. (2003) describe a case where effective stress parameters back-calculated from static load tests were much lower than expected because of artesian conditions. A detailed subsurface exploration can identify them; designs whose nominal resistance needs pile lengths that punch through confining layers should be avoided, and artesian conditions should be noted on the foundation plans.

subsections.title: Scour
subsections.body: Scour at bridge foundations removes soil around piles, reducing shaft resistance and lateral support. Design must account for both long-term aggradation/degradation and contraction/local scour. AASHTO requires piles be designed for the full depth of scour at the design flood (100-year) for strength limit and check flood (500-year) for extreme event.
key_points: Three scour components: long-term degradation, contraction scour, local scour
Strength limit: full scour depth at design flood (100-year)
Extreme event: full scour at check flood (500-year), see Section 7.4
Shaft resistance lost in scour zone must be subtracted from total resistance
Lateral support lost in scour zone increases pile unsupported length
Must evaluate stream migration potential
Refer to HEC-18 (Arneson et al. 2012) for scour depth calculation
figures: Figure 7-36: Scour effects on pile resistance and lateral support

subsections.title: Downdrag
subsections.body: Downdrag occurs when soil around a pile settles more than the pile, applying downward drag force (negative shaft resistance). The drag force acts as an additional load on the pile and must be considered in the strength limit state. Common causes include consolidation of soft clays under fill, lowering of the groundwater table, and settlement of liquefied soils after an earthquake. The neutral plane is the depth where the pile and soil settlement are equal.
key_points: Downdrag = negative shaft resistance from soil settling more than the pile
Treated as additional factored load, NOT reduced resistance per AASHTO
Drag load computed using alpha method (cohesive) or beta method (cohesionless)
Neutral plane: depth where pile and soil settlement are equal
Common causes: fill on soft clay, GWT lowering, adjacent surcharge, liquefaction
Bitumen coatings can reduce downdrag but reduce positive shaft resistance too
See Section 7.3.6 for service limit state downdrag (settlement-based approach)

Figure 7-28: Neutral plane concept for downdrag

sections.title: Service Limit States
sections.summary: Service checks: settlement, horizontal movement, rotation, overall stability, and deformation with scour at the design flood (100-year), using Service I loads. Moulton's limiting angular distortion (Table 7-18): 0.004 multi-span, 0.005 simple-span (longitudinal only); lateral movement 1.5 in. The S-0 concept (Duncan and Tan 1991): one support may settle the computed amount while the next does not. Group settlement: elastic compression, Meyerhof SPT/CPT (cohesionless), equivalent footing (cohesive), Janbu tangent modulus, neutral plane; downdrag; p-y lateral deflection.
sections.body: 7.3 Service Limit States (p. 308). Service limit states for foundations include settlement, lateral movement, overall stability and scour at the design flood. Foundation movement should be limited to structural tolerances for both total and differential deformations; as AASHTO (2014) notes, the economics of limiting settlement, rotation and horizontal movement should be compared with the cost of designing the superstructure to tolerate the movement, including maintenance of structural or roadway elements. Deformations should be computed assuming scour will occur at the design flood. The service limit state provides limits on stress, deformation and cracking under regular service conditions; its geotechnical considerations for driven piles are vertical deformation (settlement), horizontal movements, rotation, overall stability, and deformations due to scour at the design flood (100 year event). Settlements should be determined with the Service I load combination, which includes normal operational factors only; for pile foundations in or on cohesive deposits subject to time dependent consolidation settlement, transient loads may be excluded from the settlement analysis (methods in Section 7.3.5). Load combinations for all applicable service limit states should be evaluated for horizontal movement and foundation rotation. Horizontal movement is measured at the foundation top and should be within structural limits based on column length and stiffness; sufficient geotechnical resistance and structural stiffness to resist shear and overturning loads should be checked (lateral loading in Section 7.3.7). Rotation is likewise measured at the foundation top and should be restricted. See AASHTO (2014) Articles 10.5.2.1 through 10.5.2.4 and commentary; all applicable service limit state load combinations must be evaluated. Subsections: 7.3.1 Tolerable Vertical Deformations and Angular Distortion; 7.3.2 S-0 Concept for Vertical Deformations; 7.3.3 Construction Point Concept; 7.3.4 Recommended Procedure for Vertical Deformation Analysis; 7.3.5 Pile Group Settlement; 7.3.6 Settlement Due to Downdrag; 7.3.7 Horizontal Pile Foundation Deflection; 7.3.8 Lateral Squeeze of Foundation Soil and Solutions; 7.3.9 Overall Stability.
key_points: Service limit states: settlement, lateral movement, rotation, overall stability and design flood scour
Limit total and differential movement to structural tolerances
Weigh the cost of limiting movement against designing the superstructure to tolerate it (AASHTO 2014)
Compute deformations assuming scour at the design flood (100 year event)
Settlement with the Service I load combination; transient loads may be excluded for consolidating cohesive deposits
Horizontal movement and rotation at the foundation top, within structural limits
Evaluate all applicable service load combinations (AASHTO 2014 Articles 10.5.2.1 to 10.5.2.4)

subsections.title: Tolerable Deformations
subsections.body: Establishes tolerable deformation criteria for pile-supported structures. Angular distortion (differential settlement / span length) is the primary criterion. For bridges, AASHTO (2014) recommends angular distortion limits. Total settlement limits depend on structure type and function.
key_points: Angular distortion = differential settlement / span length
AASHTO bridge limit: angular distortion < 0.004 for multi-span bridges
Single span bridges more tolerant: angular distortion < 0.008
Total settlement typically 25-50 mm for bridges on piles
Lateral deflection limits depend on structural requirements and utility connections
Table 7-18 provides tolerable movement criteria for various structure types
figures: Figure 7-37: Angular distortion definition and tolerable limits
tables: Table 7-18: Tolerable movement criteria for highway bridges and structures

subsections.title: S-0 Concept (Load-Settlement Behavior)
subsections.body: The S-0 (load-settlement) concept describes the relationship between applied load and pile head settlement. Settlement includes elastic compression of the pile, movement of the pile toe into the soil, and elastic compression of the soil beneath the pile toe. The shape of the S-0 curve depends on whether the pile is friction or end-bearing dominated.
key_points: S-0 curve: complete load vs settlement relationship for a pile
Three settlement components: pile elastic compression, toe movement, soil compression below toe
Friction piles: gradual curving S-0 with large elastic compression
End-bearing piles: stiff response until toe capacity mobilized, then rapid settlement
Davisson offset method defines failure load from S-0 curve
Typical failure settlement = pile elastic compression + 4.0 mm + D/120
figures: Figure 7-38: Typical S-0 curves for friction and end-bearing piles
Figure 7-39: Davisson failure criterion applied to S-0 curve

subsections.title: Construction Point Concept
subsections.body: The construction point concept recognizes that some settlement occurs during construction before the superstructure is connected. Settlement occurring before the connection is made does not affect the structure. Design should evaluate settlement under incremental loading at each construction stage.
key_points: Settlement before superstructure connection does not affect angular distortion
Construction sequence timing affects how much settlement impacts the structure
Incremental loading analysis recommended for each construction stage
Figure 7-40: Construction point concept illustration
Particularly important for approach fills on soft ground
figures: Figure 7-40: Construction point concept for settlement evaluation
Figure 7-41: Example construction sequence with settlement stages

subsections.title: Recommended Procedure for Settlement Analysis
subsections.body: Recommends a systematic procedure for evaluating pile group settlement, considering the construction sequence, load increments, and appropriate analysis methods based on soil type.
key_points: Step 1: Determine construction sequence and load increments
Step 2: Estimate elastic compression of pile
Step 3: Estimate group settlement below pile toe using appropriate method
Step 4: Sum components and compare to tolerable limits
Select analysis method based on soil type and available data

subsections.title: Pile Group Settlement
subsections.body: Presents methods for estimating settlement of pile groups, which is generally larger than single pile settlement due to the increased zone of influence. The equivalent footing approach models the group as a shallow footing at some depth below the pile toe level. Different methods are used for cohesionless and cohesive soils.
key_points: Group settlement typically 1.5-3x single pile settlement for friction piles
End-bearing groups on rock or dense sand may have settlement = single pile settlement
Equivalent footing concept: group modeled as footing at 2/3 pile embedment depth
Cohesionless soils: Meyerhof SPT and CPT methods (semi-empirical)
Cohesive soils: equivalent footing with consolidation analysis
Janbu tangent modulus method as general alternative
Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement

subsections.title: Elastic Compression of Pile
subsections.body: Elastic compression of the pile itself is a significant component of total pile head settlement, particularly for long piles. It depends on the load distribution along the pile, the pile cross-section, and the elastic modulus of the pile material.
key_points: Elastic compression = P*L / (A*E) for uniform load (end-bearing)
For friction piles: 0.5 * P*L / (A*E) since load decreases linearly with depth
Composite piles: sum elastic compression of each material segment
Can be 10-30 mm or more for long piles
equations: Eq 7-48: delta_e = P*L / (A*E) (elastic compression, end bearing)
Eq 7-49: delta_e = 0.5 * P*L / (A*E) (elastic compression, uniform shaft resistance)
figures: Figure 7-42: Load distribution assumptions for elastic compression calculation

subsections.title: Settlement of Pile Groups in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: For pile groups in cohesionless soils, the Meyerhof (1976) SPT and CPT methods provide semi-empirical estimates of group settlement. These methods correlate group settlement to the group load, group dimensions, and in-situ test data. The SPT method uses corrected N60 values and the CPT method uses average cone tip resistance in the influence zone below the pile toe.
key_points: Meyerhof SPT method: s = (q_net * B_g * I) / (N60_bar) (Eq 7-50)
Meyerhof CPT method: s = (q_net * B_g * I) / (2 * q_c_bar) (Eq 7-52)
Influence factor I = 1 - D / (8 * B_g) >= 0.5
Average N60 or q_c from pile toe to B_g below pile toe
Settlement increases with group width and applied stress
Typically provides reasonable estimates for normally consolidated sands
equations: Eq 7-50: s = q * sqrt(B_g) / (0.96 * N60_bar) (Meyerhof SPT settlement, mm)
Eq 7-51: I = 1 - D / (8 * B_g) >= 0.5 (depth influence factor)
Eq 7-52: s = q * sqrt(B_g) / (2 * q_c_bar) (Meyerhof CPT settlement, mm)
Eq 7-53: B_g = (n-1)*s + b (group width, where s = pile spacing, b = pile diameter)
Eq 7-54: q = Q_g / (B_g * Z_g) (average applied stress on equivalent footing)
figures: Figure 7-43: Equivalent footing concept for pile group in cohesionless soil

subsections.title: Settlement of Pile Groups in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: For pile groups in cohesive soils, the equivalent footing method places the footing at 2/3 of the pile embedment depth. The load spreads at 2V:1H below the equivalent footing. Consolidation settlement is computed for each sublayer using the compression index Cc or recompression index Cr. The method accounts for preconsolidation pressure to distinguish between normally consolidated and overconsolidated conditions.
key_points: Equivalent footing at 2/3 pile embedment depth (D_b = 2D/3)
Load spreads at 2V:1H below equivalent footing
Settlement computed layer by layer using Cc/(1+e0) * log10(sigma'_f/sigma'_0)
NC soils: use Cc; OC soils: use Cr up to preconsolidation pressure, then Cc
Stress distribution computed at midpoint of each sublayer
Total settlement = sum of sublayer settlements
Must check influence depth (10% of overburden stress increase)
equations: Eq 7-55: s = SUM[Cc_i/(1+e0_i) * H_i * log10(sigma'_f_i / sigma'_0_i)] (NC settlement)
Eq 7-56: s = SUM[Cr_i/(1+e0_i) * H_i * log10(sigma'_f_i / sigma'_0_i)] (OC settlement, sigma'_f < sigma'_p)
Eq 7-57: s = SUM[Cr_i/(1+e0_i)*H_i*log10(sigma'_p_i/sigma'_0_i) + Cc_i/(1+e0_i)*H_i*log10(sigma'_f_i/sigma'_p_i)] (OC becoming NC)
Eq 7-58: Delta_sigma_v = Q_g / ((B_g + z_i)*(Z_g + z_i)) (stress increase at depth z_i below equivalent footing)

subsections.title: Time Rate of Settlement
subsections.body: For cohesive soils, consolidation settlement occurs over time as excess pore water pressures dissipate. The time rate is governed by the coefficient of consolidation cv, the drainage path length, and the drainage conditions (single or double drainage).
key_points: Degree of consolidation U(t) from Terzaghi 1-D consolidation theory
Time factor Tv = cv * t / H_dr^2
Double drainage: H_dr = H/2; single drainage: H_dr = H
90% consolidation typically used for design
Horizontal drainage (radial consolidation) can accelerate settlement
cv from laboratory consolidation tests (odometer) or back-calculated from field data
equations: Eq 7-59: T_v = c_v * t / H_dr^2 (time factor for consolidation)

subsections.title: Settlement in Layered Soils
subsections.body: For layered soil profiles, settlement is computed separately for each layer and summed. The stress distribution must account for load spreading through different soil types.

subsections.title: Janbu Tangent Modulus Method
subsections.body: The Janbu (1963, 1967) tangent modulus method provides an alternative approach for settlement estimation using the tangent constrained modulus M = 1/mv as a function of stress level. The method is applicable to all soil types and uses a modulus number m and stress exponent j to characterize the soil compressibility.
key_points: Alternative to Cc/Cr approach; applicable to all soil types
Tangent constrained modulus M = 1/m_v varies with stress level
Three soil types: j=0 (normally consolidated clay), j=0.5 (silt/sand), j=1 (dense sand/till)
Modulus number m from Table 7-20 based on soil type and density
Method accounts for stress-dependent compressibility
Particularly useful for mixed or non-standard soil profiles
equations: Eq 7-60: epsilon = integral of d_sigma / M(sigma) (strain from stress increase)
Eq 7-61: M = m * sigma_r * (sigma'_v / sigma_r)^(1-j) for j > 0 (tangent modulus)
Eq 7-62: M = m * sigma_r / (1 + e_0) for j = 0 (NC clay tangent modulus)
Eq 7-63: epsilon = (1/m) * ln(sigma'_f / sigma'_0) for j = 0 (NC clay strain)
Eq 7-64: epsilon = (2/m) * [sqrt(sigma'_f/sigma_r) - sqrt(sigma'_0/sigma_r)] for j = 0.5 (silt strain)
Eq 7-65: epsilon = (1/m) * (sigma'_f - sigma'_0) / sigma_r for j = 1 (dense sand strain)
Eq 7-66: s = SUM(epsilon_i * H_i) (total settlement from strain and layer thickness)
Eq 7-67: OC strain uses reloading modulus number m_r
Eq 7-68: For OC soil becoming NC: strain = OC part + NC part
Eq 7-69: sigma_r = 100 kPa (reference stress)

subsections.title: Neutral Plane Method for Settlement
subsections.body: The neutral plane method (Fellenius 1989, 2004) provides a rational approach for evaluating pile settlement considering the load transfer mechanism along the pile. The neutral plane is the depth where the relative pile-soil movement is zero. Above the neutral plane, the soil settles more than the pile (negative shaft resistance/downdrag). Below the neutral plane, the pile settles more than the soil (positive shaft resistance). Settlement is computed at the neutral plane depth.
key_points: Neutral plane: depth where pile and soil settlement are equal
Above neutral plane: soil settles more than pile (negative shaft resistance)
Below neutral plane: pile settles more than soil (positive shaft resistance)
Settlement at neutral plane = pile elastic compression + toe movement
Method integrates strength and service limit states into single framework
Figure 7-49 illustrates the unified neutral plane diagram
figures: Figure 7-49: Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement evaluation

subsections.title: Downdrag Settlement
subsections.body: Addresses the service limit state evaluation of downdrag, where the pile settlement due to downdrag forces must be within tolerable limits. The neutral plane approach is used to compute settlement rather than treating downdrag as additional load (which is the strength limit state approach).
key_points: Service limit state: downdrag evaluated as settlement, not additional load
Neutral plane method (Fellenius 1989, Siegel 2013) for settlement computation
Settlement = pile compression above neutral plane + toe settlement
Bitumen coatings reduce downdrag forces but also reduce positive shaft resistance
Must check both strength (drag load) and service (settlement) limit states
equations: Eq 7-70: s_downdrag = delta_pile + delta_toe (total downdrag settlement)
Eq 7-71: delta_pile = integral(P(z)/(A*E)) dz from 0 to neutral plane (pile elastic compression)
Eq 7-72: delta_toe = f(Q_toe, soil stiffness) (toe settlement from load transfer)
figures: Figure 7-50: Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement

subsections.title: Neutral Plane Approach for Downdrag
subsections.body: The neutral plane is found by constructing the load distribution along the pile from both the top (dead load + drag force) and bottom (toe + positive shaft resistance). The intersection defines the neutral plane depth.

subsections.title: Settlement Computation
subsections.body: Once the neutral plane is located, the pile settlement is computed as the sum of elastic pile compression from the pile head to the neutral plane and the toe settlement. The toe settlement can be estimated from load-transfer curves or published correlations.

subsections.title: Lateral Deflection Analysis
subsections.body: Covers methods for evaluating lateral deflection of single piles and pile groups under lateral loads. The p-y method is the primary approach, modeling the soil-pile interaction using nonlinear springs (p-y curves) along the pile length. Group effects are accounted for using p-multipliers that reduce the p-y spring stiffness for piles within a group. The strain wedge method is also discussed as an alternative approach.
key_points: p-y method is the primary lateral analysis approach
p-y curves model nonlinear soil-pile interaction springs
Different p-y curves for different soil types (soft clay, stiff clay, sand)
Fixed vs free head conditions significantly affect deflection and moment
Group effects via p-multipliers (0.2-1.0 depending on position and spacing)
Leading row piles have higher p-multipliers than trailing rows
Strain wedge method suitable for short stiff piles
Computer programs: LPILE, COM624P, GROUP, FB-MultiPier
equations: Eq 7-73: EI * d4y/dx4 + P_x * d2y/dx2 - p = 0 (beam on nonlinear foundation differential equation)

Figure 7-52: Single pile p-y model (beam on nonlinear springs)

subsections.title: Pile Head Fixity
subsections.body: The degree of rotational restraint at the pile head (fixed, free, or partial fixity) significantly affects the lateral deflection and bending moment distribution. Fixed head conditions reduce deflection but increase the negative moment at the pile head. Free head conditions allow rotation and result in larger deflection but lower pile head moments.

subsections.title: Lateral Design Methods Overview
subsections.body: Two primary methods for lateral pile analysis: the p-y method (most common for long flexible piles) and the strain wedge method (better for short stiff piles). The p-y method models the pile as a beam on nonlinear springs. The strain wedge method computes passive soil resistance using a 3D failure wedge.

subsections.title: p-y Method
subsections.body: The p-y method solves the beam-on-nonlinear-foundation differential equation (Eq 7-73) using iterative finite difference techniques. Different p-y curve formulations are used for different soil types: Matlock (1970) for soft clay, Reese et al. (1975) for stiff clay below water table, Welch and Reese (1972) for stiff clay above water table, Reese et al. (1974) for sand, and API (1993) for sand. Software programs LPILE and COM624P automate this analysis.
key_points: Beam on nonlinear foundation: EI*d4y/dx4 + Px*d2y/dx2 - p = 0
Matlock (1970): soft clay below water table
Reese et al. (1975): stiff clay below water table
Welch and Reese (1972): stiff clay above water table
Reese et al. (1974): sand
API (1993): sand (alternative to Reese et al.)
Evans and Duncan (1982): weak rock
Iterative solution by finite difference method
Results: deflection, moment, shear, and soil reaction profiles

subsections.title: Strain Wedge Method
subsections.body: The strain wedge method (Norris 1986, Ashour et al. 1998) models the soil failure around a laterally loaded pile using a three-dimensional passive wedge. It relates the horizontal soil resistance to the horizontal strain in the passive wedge and provides p-y curves as output. The method is particularly suitable for short stiff piles and layered soils.

subsections.title: Single Pile Lateral Analysis
subsections.body: For single piles, the p-y analysis determines the lateral deflection, rotation, bending moment, shear force, and soil reaction distribution along the pile length. The analysis is performed for each load combination (service, strength, extreme event). Critical output includes maximum deflection (usually at pile head) and maximum bending moment (usually 3-8 pile diameters below ground).

subsections.title: Pile Group Lateral Analysis
subsections.body: For pile groups under lateral loading, the p-y curves are modified using p-multipliers to account for pile-soil-pile interaction (shadowing) effects. Leading row piles have higher p-multipliers than trailing rows because they push into undisturbed soil. P-multipliers depend on pile spacing, number of rows, and row position. Brown et al. (1988) and others have developed p-multiplier values from full-scale lateral load tests.

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit States
sections.summary: Extreme events (low probability; protect against collapse): check flood scour (500-year; deeper scour prism, unfactored loads, phi = 1.0 for axial compression and lateral, 0.8 or less for uplift), vessel and vehicle collision, seismic loading (liquefaction, ground movement, seismic loads and drag force; detailed seismic design in GEC-3), ice and debris, and other site-specific events; combined extreme events in 7.4.4.
sections.body: 7.4 Extreme Event Limit States (p. 376). Extreme event limit states involve events with a low probability of occurrence that can still harm the foundation and structure if not considered in design; as AASHTO (2014) notes, the extreme event limit state exists to protect against structural collapse and preserve life. AASHTO (2014) gives guidance on extreme event loading cases including ice loading and vehicle and vessel impacts; Arneson et al. (2012) details scour near bridge piers and abutments; Kavazanjian et al. (2011) discusses seismic events in depth; background on ice loads is in Montgomery et al. (1984); vessel impact design is in the AASHTO (2009) Guide Specifications and Commentary for Vessel Collision Design of Highway Bridges. Extreme event evaluations ensure structural survival of a bridge under unique major occurrences such as earthquakes, floods and vehicle or vessel collisions with return periods significantly greater than the bridge design life. Extreme event limit states for driven pile foundation design include: the check flood for scour; vessel collision; vehicle collision; seismic loading; ice and debris loading; and other site-specific situations determined by the design engineer. Subsections: 7.4.1 Extreme Event Scour During Check Flood; 7.4.2 Seismic and Seismic Induced Downdrag; 7.4.3 Ice and Collisions; 7.4.4 Combined Extreme Events.

sections.title: Determination of Minimum Pile Penetration
sections.summary: Settlement and structure deformation must stay within tolerable limits (Section 7.3.1). After all limit state analyses, specify a minimum pile penetration only if needed; often an estimated length suffices. Per AASHTO (2014) it is the toe elevation needed for single pile and group settlement, lateral deflection, uplift, drag force from static settlement, liquefaction, axial and lateral resistance after scour, fixity for lateral loads (AASHTO is silent on how fixity is defined), and extreme event uplift and lateral loads. Check with a wave equation drivability analysis during design; if it cannot be reached, use another pile type or installation aids.
sections.body: 7.5 Determination of Minimum Pile Penetration (pp. 388-389). Foundation settlement and the resulting structure deformation should be kept within tolerable limits (Section 7.3.1). Once all limit state analyses have been performed, minimum pile penetration depths should be specified, if necessary; they may be required to limit structure vertical or lateral deformations under applied loads. A minimum penetration should be specified only if needed: in many cases an estimated length alone is satisfactory, recognizing that once piles achieve their required nominal driving resistance, driving may be terminated shorter than the estimated length. The ability of an appropriately sized hammer to drive piles to the specified minimum penetration should be evaluated during design in a wave equation drivability analysis, which checks constructability and whether the depth can be achieved; an alternative pile type or installation aids may need to be specified if it is not obtainable by conventional driving. AASHTO (2014) states that the minimum pile penetration depth shall be the pile toe elevation needed to satisfy, as applicable: (a) single pile and pile group settlement (service, Section 7.3.5); (b) lateral deflection (service, Section 7.3.7); (c) uplift (strength, Section 7.2.3); (d) penetration into soils to accommodate drag forces from static settlement stresses (service, Section 7.3.6); (e) penetration due to liquefaction (strength and extreme event, Section 7.4.2); (f) penetration for adequate axial (compression and uplift) and lateral resistance after scour (strength, Section 7.2.9; extreme event, Section 7.4.1); (g) penetration to achieve fixity for resisting applied lateral loads (strength, Section 7.2.5; service, Section 7.3.7), noting that AASHTO is silent on the definition of fixity, which varies if defined by the deflection profile, the bending moment profile or the pile head deflection; and (h) axial uplift and lateral resistance for extreme event loads (Section 7.4).
key_points: Specify a minimum penetration after all limit state analyses, and only if needed
Often an estimated length suffices; driving may stop short of it once the required nominal driving resistance is reached
Check with a wave equation drivability analysis during design; otherwise another pile type or installation aids
